newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Heating oil stocks seen turning the corner.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Heating oil stocks seen turning the corner.

text.p: Rising U.S. distillate inventories and weakening spot diesel fuel prices may signal the long-awaited start of a seasonal build in heating oil stocks, analysts said following release of the weekly American Petroleum Institute stocks survey late Tuesday.
Differentials on spot diesel barrels in the Midwest and New York Harbor fell this week on easing demand with several weeks remaining in the autumn harvest season, analysts said.
"The cash market is the first sign demand is waning," said Dee Dee Finley, a Merrill Lynch broker in Kansas City, Mo.

If it holds up, the easing demand for diesel fuel should allow refiners in the coming weeks to replenish heating oil stocks that remained 17.1 million barrels below last year's levels, according to the latest API estimates.

"I think we are starting to turn that corner here. Right now is probably the time when you start seeing some pulling back of diesel demand," said Steven Platt, energy analyst with Dean Witter in Chicago.
The API in its weekly stocks survey pegged distillate inventories at 113.65 million barrels nationwide for the week ended October 4, up 1.3 million barrels from the prior week.

Despite the build, analysts said refiners had not boosted distillate production yields. Distillate accounted for 23.7 percent of the barrel, unchanged from last week, while gasoline yields eased modestly to 51.4 percent of the barrel.
Gasoline stocks nationwide were drawn down 810,000 barrels at U.S. refineries, which reported a total 196.32 million barrels on hand in primary storage.
"Having been the dog for so long, (gasoline) actually could hold up best of the complex if we start seeing a little bit of pressure coming into the crude or the heat," Platt said.
Crude inventories were drawn down by 798,000 barrels on the week, leaving stocks on hand in primary storage at the nation's refineries at 302.30 million barrels, API said.

The crude oil draw occured despite a drop in refinery runs and a surge in oil imports. Crude runs eased 0.6 percentage points on the week, with U.S. refineries operating at a brisk 94.9 percent of capacity, API said.
Crude imports for the week ended October 4 stood at 7.89 million barrels, rising an average 1.35 million barrels per day while product imports were up a modest 178,000 barrels per day, API said.
